paper.title: Socioeconomic background affects mortality in Danish children with severe chronic disease
paper.code_data_availability: No data- or code-availability statement is printed. The paper states only: …

registers.role: sample frame / exposure (identification of severe chronic disease and disease category)
variables_mentioned: specific diagnosis codes registered in relation to hospitalisations

registers.role: treatment / controls (socioeconomic information: maternal and paternal age, siblings, living with both parents, family income, maternal and paternal education, maternal and paternal job status)
variables_mentioned: Family income (population adjusted to calendar year)

registers.name_in_paper: Danish national registers (the Danish civil registration system, cited as ref. 8)

linkages: Children born in Denmark 1994-2018 linked to diagnoses in the National Patient Register 1994-2020

Children linked to parental and family socioeconomic information obtained from Statistics Denmark (maternal and paternal age, education and job status, family income, siblings, living with both parents)
Children linked to the Cause of Death Register for mortality ascertainment

sample.unit_of_observation: child (one record per child, followed from the date of initial diagnosis)
selection_rules: Background population: all children born in Denmark 1994-2018
Exposure and outcome ascertained in the period 1994-2020
Children with severe chronic disease identified in the National Patient Register using specific diagnosis codes registered in relation to hospitalisations
Diagnoses divided into 11 categories based on ICD-10 chapters (Table 1)
Followed from the date of initial diagnosis to the first of: death, emigration, 18 years of age or 31 December 2020
Post-discharge mortality analysis: deaths occurring in the hospital before discharge to the home after birth excluded

In the main analysis children contributed only with the first occurring diagnosis; in the disease-category sub-analyses children with diagnoses in more than one category could contribute to more than one sub-analysis
In the direct cancer vs. non-cancer comparison the child belonged only to the group in which it was first diagnosed
sample.n_observations: 128 129 children (3521 deaths) in the total-mortality analysis; 127 224 children (2639 deaths) in the post-discharge-mortality analysis
sample.n_individuals: 128 129 children with chronic disease, of which 11 461 (8.9%) of non-Danish ethnicity (69 435 male and 58 694 female)

construction_notes: The 10 socioeconomic factors and their levels are listed in Table 2; each was included as a categorical covariate.
All analyses were adjusted for age at diagnosis and calendar time as continuous covariates measured in years and stratified for seasonality.
Missing values were handled by allocating a separate covariate level.

The socioeconomic risk score was generated as the sum of the individual socioeconomic factors weighted by the estimated coefficients from the main model, and the result was scaled by log(2) so that the hazard ratio is the relative change in the mortality rate when the risk score is doubled.
Two versions of each model were fitted: one with ethnicity status (Danish or non-Danish) as a covariate, and one separated by ethnicity.
Within each chronic disease category the risk score entered as a continuous covariate, with an interaction term with ethnicity status when relevant.
The cancer vs. non-cancer contrast was assessed by introducing an additional interaction term for cancer vs. non-cancer.
Two mortality outcomes: total mortality and post-discharge mortality (excluding deaths in the hospital before discharge to the home after birth).
Median age at first diagnosis 1.42 years (range 0-18 years).

links.pointer_quote: Overall, non-Danish ethnicity (HR = 1.96 (95% CI 1.69–2.28)) was associated with all-cause mortality in 128 129 children (69 435 male and 58 694 female) with chronic disease.

claims.statement: Among children born in Denmark 1994-2018 with a severe chronic disease, 'Non-Danish ethnicity' is associated with a higher mortality rate (total mortality, overall model with ethnicity status as a covariate).

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark (socioeconomic information; the specific register and variable names are not given)

definition.value: Indicator for non-Danish ethnicity status; entered as a categorical covariate in the overall ('main analysis') Cox model. The paper does not print the algorithm defining ethnicity status.

register_source.value: The Cause of Death Register (no DST variable names given)

definition.value: All-cause death. Children were followed from the date of initial diagnosis to the first of: death, emigration, 18 years of age or 31 December 2020; mortality was ascertained from the Cause of Death Register. Analysed by Cox regression with time to death as the outcome and time since diagnosis as the underlying time scale.

timing.value: Time to death measured from the date of initial diagnosis; follow-up ends at death, emigration, age 18 or 31 December 2020.

units.value: hazard ratio: the mortality rate relative to the reference level

magnitude.interpretation: non-Danish ethnicity was the single factor with the largest impact on the mortality rate in the overall model

estimand.target_population: All children born in Denmark 1994-2018 with a severe chronic disease diagnosed in the National Patient Register 1994-2020; ethnicity status enters the model as a covariate ('main analysis').
estimand.time_horizon: the whole follow-up from the date of initial diagnosis until death, emigration, 18 years of age or 31 December 2020

population.description: All children born in Denmark 1994-2018 with a severe chronic disease diagnosed in the National Patient Register 1994-2020; ethnicity status enters the model as a covariate ('main analysis').
population.ages: 0-18 years (follow-up censored at 18 years of age); median age at first diagnosis 1.42 years
subgroups_defined: 11 categories of chronic disease based on ICD-10 chapters (Table 1)
population.selection: Children identified as having a severe chronic disease from specific diagnosis codes registered in relation to hospitalisations in the National Patient Register; the cohort is conditioned on having such a diagnosis.

identification.source_of_variation: None exploited: an observational national cohort. The contrast is between children whose families differ in the socioeconomic characteristic, with adjustment for the covariates in the Cox model; no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used.

key_assumptions.assumption: Proportional hazards: the hazard ratio for each covariate is constant over time since diagnosis (the Cox model is fitted with the baseline hazard stratified for seasonality).
Complete and accurate register ascertainment of diagnoses, socioeconomic background and deaths, with no loss to follow-up.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors name complete coverage and no loss to follow-up, attributed to the quality of the Danish health and social registers, as a strength of the study.

key_assumptions.assumption: Missing covariate values are handled by allocating a separate covariate level; the authors state that missingness cannot be assumed to be (completely) random.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No sensitivity analysis for missingness is reported; the authors list it as a limitation.

key_assumptions.assumption: Non-informative censoring: censoring at emigration, 18 years of age or 31 December 2020 is independent of the mortality hazard given the covariates.
The paper frames the estimates as associations and states no condition under which the adjusted hazard ratio would equal a causal effect; no unconfoundedness assumption is asserted.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The aim is stated as assessing 'the association between socioeconomic factors and mortality'; the results and conclusion use 'associated with' throughout.

threats_discussed: Missing data: the authors state that missingness cannot be assumed to be (completely) random
Training and validation data sets were not used in the model fit prior to the calculation of the risk scores
Minor overlap: children could contribute to more than one sub-analysis across the different categories of chronic diagnoses
Many childhood deaths were not covered, in particular deaths in children without a severe chronic diagnosis
robustness_checks: Two mortality outcomes analysed: total mortality and post-discharge mortality (excluding deaths in hospital before discharge to the home after birth)
Two versions of each model fitted: one with ethnicity status as a covariate and one separated by ethnicity status
unresolved_confounders: Missing data, which the authors state cannot be assumed to be (completely) random
